reception.text: The Salt Lake Herald greeted the news on page one under the headline "PRESERVED FROM VANDALS."
Within a day the Salt Lake Tribune called the reservation too small, opening a run of at least four editorials in twelve days.
Byron Cummings, whose 1907 survey underlay the proclamation, told a Salt Lake paper the reservation was not sufficient for its purpose.
The Tribune proposed enlarging the monument to a full township, six miles square, or 23,040 acres.
The Salt Lake Real Estate Association formally petitioned for a full-township reserve.
The Utah press almost uniformly reported the monument as forty acres rather than 120, so critics argued against a reservation one-third its true size.
The Tribune observed that no one opposed the reservation because there were no conflicting interests, vested rights, or settlements on the ground.
The Tribune reported a proclamation adding a tract nine by fourteen miles; no such proclamation was issued.

political_impact.text: Roosevelt asked Gifford Pinchot how much more land was needed, with Senator Reed Smoot working the question in Washington.
General Land Office surveyor William B. Douglass resurveyed the area and had the bridges given Hopi-word names, which the U.S. Geographic Board accepted: Sipapu, Kachina, and Owachomo.

legacy.text: Taft's 1909 proclamation replaced the three forty-acre squares with about 2,740 acres, a direct answer to the 1908 campaign for more land.
The Geographic Board's Fourth and Fifth Reports paired two of the new names with the wrong bridges until the Board re-decided all three in 1937.
Natural Bridges was certified as the world's first International Dark Sky Park.

today.name: Natural Bridges National Monument
today.note: Utah's first national monument and the state's first unit of the national park system; about 7,636 acres today.
today.source: NPS Land Resources Division, listing of acreage, June 30, 2026

related.note: Grand Canyon, three months earlier, read the Antiquities Act's smallest-area clause to cover more than 800,000 acres; Natural Bridges read it literally.

later_actions.text: Proclamation 881 enlarged the monument to about 2,740 acres.
Proclamation 1323 re-described the boundary against new survey corners without enlarging it.
The U.S. Geographic Board re-decided the names Sipapu, Kachina, and Owachomo.
Proclamation 3486 added about 5,236 acres and excluded about 320 acres at Snow Flat Spring Cave and Cigarette Spring Cave.

uncertain: Whether Douglass found the earlier names attached to the wrong bridges, as is often said, is unconfirmed; the only firsthand account reports just an objection to the names.
